¶
'''bless'''<sup>2</sup>† (bles), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' [< ME. ''blessen'', ''blyssen'', ''blechen'', strike, wound, < OF. ''blecier'', ''blechier'', F. ''blesser'', wound, injure; of uncertain origin, perhaps < MHG. ''ze-bletzen'', cut to pieces, < ''ze-'', G. ''zer-'' (= AS. ''tō-'', E. ''to-''<sup>2</sup>), apart, + ''bletz'', ''blez'', OHG. ''bletz'', a patch, a piece.] '''1.''' To wound; hurt; beat; thump. ''Skelton.''—'''2.''' [Appar. a deflection of sense 1. Some fancy that it refers to “the old rite of blessing a field by directing the hands to all parts of it” (see ''bless''<sup>1</sup>).] To wave; brandish.
{{smaller block|<poem>He priked in formest
& ''blessed'' so with his briȝt bront aboute in eche side
That what rink so he rauȝt he ros never after.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'', l. 1191.}}
His sparkling blade about his head he ''blest.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 22.}}}}

'''blessbok''', ''n.'' See ''blesbok''.

'''blessed''' (bles′ed or blest; as pret. and pp. commonly pronounced ''blest'', and often so written), ''p. a.'' [Pp. of ''bless''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Consecrated; holy: as, the ''blessed'' sacrament.
{{smaller block|I . . . dipped my finger in the ''blessed'' water.
{{right|''Marryat'', Phantom Ship, i. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Worthy of adoration: as, the ''blessed'' Trinity.
{{smaller block|<poem>O run, prevent them with thy humble ode,
And lay it lowly at his ''blessed'' feet.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 25.}}
<poem>Jesus, the Christ of God,
The Father’s ''blessed'' Son.</poem>
{{right|''Bonar'', Hymns of Faith and Hope.}}}}
'''3.''' Enjoying supreme happiness or felicity; favored with blessings; highly favored; happy; fortunate: as, “England’s ''blessed'' shore,” ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2; the ''blessedest'' of mortals.

{{smaller block|Its [the medlar’s] fruit is hard, acid, and unfit for eating till it loses its green colour and becomes ''bletted.''

'''bletonist''' (blet′ọn-ist), ''n.'' [See ''bletonism''.] One who possesses or pretends to possess the faculty of bletonism.

'''bletting''' (blet′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''blet'', ''v.''] The slow internal decay or “sleepiness” that takes place in some fruits, as apples and pears, after they are gathered. ''Lindley.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bless|586|blight}}</noinclude>by some specified means: as, ''blessed'' with a good constitution; ''blessed'' with filial children.
{{smaller block|You will to your lute, I heard you could touch it cunningly; pray ''bless'' my ears a little.
{{right|''Shirley'', Witty Fair One, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mrs. Bull . . . ''blessed'' John with three daughters.
{{right|''Arbuthnot'', John Bull (1755), p. 30. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''8.''' To praise or extol (''a'') as holy or worthy of reverence, or (''b'') as the giver of benefits; extol or glorify with thankful acknowledgment of benefits received.
{{smaller block|''Bless'' the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, ''bless'' His holy name.
{{right|Ps. ciii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|I am content with this, and ''bless'' my fortune.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iii. 1.}}}}
'''9.''' To esteem or account happy; congratulate; felicitate: used reflexively.
{{smaller block|The nations shall ''bless themselves'' in him.
{{right|Jer. iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Bless'' not ''thyself'' only that thou wert born in Athens.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., i. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Often used in exclamations with various shades of meaning departing more or less widely from the literal sense: as, God ''bless'' me! ''bless'' you! ''bless'' the mark! etc.]—'''God bless the mark.''' See ''mark.''—'''Not to have a penny to bless one’s self with,''' to be penniless: in allusion to the cross on the silver penny (cf. Ger. ''Kreuzer''), or to the practice of crossing the palm with a piece of silver. ''N. E. D.''—'''To be blessed,''' a euphemism for ''to be damned:'' as, I’''m blessed'' if he didn’t run away; I’''m blessed'' if I know. [Slang.]}}
{{smaller block|I’''m blessed'' if I don’t expect the cur back to-morrow morning.
{{right|''Marryat'', Snarleyyow, II. xi.}}}}
{{smaller block|An emphatic and earnest desire ''to be blessed'' if she would.
{{right|''Dickens'', Oliver Twist, xiii.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''To bless one’s self.''' (''a'') To felicitate one’s self; exult. (''b'') To ejaculate “Bless me,” “God bless me,” or the like.—'''To bless one’s stars,''' to congratulate or felicitate one’s self.}}

'''bless'''<sup>2</sup>† (bles), ''v. t.'' and ''i.''   [< ME. ''blessen'', ''blyssen'', ''blechen'', strike, wound, < OF. ''blecier'', ''blechier'', F. ''blesser'', wound, injure; of uncertain origin, perhaps < MHG. ''ze-bletzen'', cut to pieces, < ''ze-'', G. ''zer-'' (= AS. ''tō-'', E. ''to-''<sup>2</sup>), apart, + ''bletz'', ''blez'', OHG. ''bletz'', a patch, a piece.]   '''1.''' To wound; hurt; beat; thump.   ''Skelton.''—'''2.''' [Appar. a deflection of sense 1. Some fancy that it refers to “the old rite of blessing a field by directing the hands to all parts of it” (see ''bless''<sup>1</sup>).] To wave; brandish.
{{smaller block|<poem>He priked in formest
& ''blessed'' so with his briȝt bront aboute in eche side
That what rink so he rauȝt he ros never after.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'', l. 1191.}}}}
{{smaller block|His sparkling blade about his head he ''blest.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 22.}}}}

'''blessbok''', ''n.'' See ''blesbok''.

'''blessed''' (bles′ed or blest; as pret. and pp. commonly pronounced ''blest'', and often so written), ''p. a.''   [Pp. of ''bless''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Consecrated; holy: as, the ''blessed'' sacrament.
{{smaller block|I . . . dipped my finger in the ''blessed'' water.
{{right|''Marryat'', Phantom Ship, i. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Worthy of adoration: as, the ''blessed'' Trinity.
{{smaller block|<poem>O run, prevent them with thy humble ode,
And lay it lowly at his ''blessed'' feet.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Jesus, the Christ of God,
The Father’s ''blessed'' Son.</poem>
{{right|''Bonar'', Hymns of Faith and Hope.}}}}
'''3.''' Enjoying supreme happiness or felicity; favored with blessings; highly favored; happy; fortunate: as, “England’s ''blessed'' shore,” ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2; the ''blessedest'' of mortals.

{{smaller block|The days are coming in the which they shall say, ''Blessed'' are the barren. {{right|Luke xxiii. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Farewell, lady;
Happy and ''blessed'' lady, goodness keep you!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Man never Is, but always To be, ''blest.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 96.}}}}
Specifically—'''4.''' Enjoying spiritual blessings and the favor of God; enjoying heavenly felicity; beatified.
{{smaller block|''Blessed'' are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. {{right|Mat. v. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|Reverenc’d like a ''blessed'' saint.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 3.}}}}
'''5.''' Fraught with or imparting blessings; bestowing happiness, health, or prosperity.
{{smaller block|<poem>The quality of mercy . . . is twice ''bless’d;''
It blesseth him that gives, and him that takes.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou ''blessed'' star, I thank thee for thy light.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, ii. 2.}}}}
'''6.''' Bringing happiness; pleasurable; joyful: as, a most ''blessed'' time; “a ''blessed'' sight to see,” ''Pepys'', Diary, May 23, 1660.—'''7.''' Endowed with or possessing healing virtues.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have . . . made familiar
To me and to my aid the ''bless’d'' infusions
That dwell in vegetives, in metals, stones.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iii. 2.}}}} tem of caucusing; he lost every ''blessed'' cent he had.—'''Blessed bell.''' {{smaller|See ''bell''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Blessed thistle.''' See ''thistle''.—'''The blessed,''' the saints in heaven; the beatified saints.}}
{{smaller block|The state also of ''the blessed'' in Paradise, though never so perfect, is not therefore left without discipline.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 1.}}}}

'''blessed-herb''' (bles′ed-ėrb), ''n.''   [A tr. of ML. ''herba benedicta'', > E. ''herb-bennet''.]   The common European avens, ''Geum urbanum''.

'''blessedly''' (bles′ed-li), ''adv.'' In a blessed manner; happily; in a fortunate manner; joyfully.
{{smaller block|One day we shall ''blessedly'' meet again never to depart.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.}}}}

'''blessedness''' (bles′ed-nes), ''n.''   [< ''blessed'' + ''-ness''.]   The state of being blessed; happiness; felicity; heavenly joys; the favor of God.
{{smaller block|<poem>His [Wolsey’s] overthrow heap’d happiness upon him;
For then, and not till then, he felt himself,
And found the ''blessedness'' of being little.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor lily, nor no glorious hyacinth,
Are of that sweetness, whiteness, tenderness,
Softness, and satisfying ''blessedness'',
As my Evanthe. ''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, i. 1.</poem>
It is such an one as, being begun in grace, passes into glory, ''blessedness'', and immortality. {{right|''South.''}}}}
'''Single blessedness,''' {{smaller|the unmarried state; celibacy.}}
{{smaller block|Grows, lives, and dies, in ''single blessedness''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Felicity'', ''Bliss'', etc. (see ''happiness''), joy, beatitude.}}

'''blesser''' (bles′ėr), ''n.'' One who bestows a blessing; one who blesses or causes to prosper.
{{smaller block|God, the giver of the gift, or ''blesser'' of the action.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, § 4.}}}}

'''blessfully''' (bles′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [For ''blissfully'', by confusion of ''bless''<sup>1</sup> with ''bliss;'' so ME. ''blesful'', and even ''blessedful'', as variations of ''blissful.'' See ''bless''<sup>1</sup> and ''bliss.'']   Blissfully. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Of these many are ''blessfully'' incognizant of the opinion, its import, its history, and even its name.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''blessfulness''' (bles′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [For ''blissfulness.'' Cf. ''blessfully.'']   Blissfulness.   ''Drant.'' [Rare.]

'''blessing''' (bles′ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blessinge'', ''blessunge'', etc., < AS. ''blētsung'', ''blēdsung'', verbal n. of ''blētsian'', bless: see ''bless''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The act of invoking or pronouncing happiness upon another or others; benediction. {{smaller|Specifically, in the Latin and Greek churches, the act of pronouncing a benediction on the laity or inferior clergy, performed by a bishop or other priest. In the Roman Catholic Church, the blessing is now given with all the fingers joined and extended, but formerly with the thumb and the first two fingers of the right hand extended and the two remaining fingers turned down. In the Greek Church, the thumb and the third finger of the same hand are joined, the other fingers being extended. Some Eastern writers see in this position a}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0612 c2f1.png|width=235px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Latin Church (old use). Greek Church. Position of Hand in Blessing.}}}}
{{smaller|symbol of the Greek sacred monogram of the name of Christ. In either case the three fingers (or two fingers and thumb) extended symbolize the Trinity. In the Anglican Church, either the former or the present Latin gesture is used.}}
'''2.''' The form of words used in this invocation or declaration; a (or the) benediction.—'''3.''' The bestowal of divine favor, or of hallowing, protecting, or prospering influences: as, to ask God’s ''blessing'' on any undertaking.—'''4.''' A temporal or spiritual benefit; anything which makes happy or prosperous; something to be thankful for; a boon or mercy: as, the ''blessings'' of life, of health, or of civilization; it is a ''blessing'' we fared so well.
{{smaller block|Nature’s full ''blessings'' would be well dispensed.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 772.}}}}
'''5.''' Euphemistically, a curse; a scolding; a castigation with words.—'''To ask a blessing,''' {{smaller|to say grace before a meal.}}
